en: Difficult to understand; obscure
hook: ABSTRUSE: ABSTRACT and CONFUSE.
story: The physics paper was so abstruse that even other physicists needed a week to understand its main argument. Abstruse means hard to understand. Synonyms: arcane, recondite, esoteric. On the GRE, clear writing is the opposite of abstruse.

en: Providing additional help or support
hook: AUXILIARY: AUX cable, extra support.
story: When the main power failed, the hospital's auxiliary generator started within seconds, keeping every machine running. Auxiliary means supplementary or backup. In grammar, auxiliary verbs like 'is' and 'have' help main verbs.

en: A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect
hook: CARICATURE: a CARtoon that exaggerates.
story: The street artist drew a caricature of Rafi: huge head, giant glasses, and tiny body. Everyone laughed, including Rafi. A caricature exaggerates features. A caricature of justice is a distorted, ridiculous version of it.

en: Moral corruption; wickedness
hook: DEPRAVITY: DEPRIVED of all goodness.
story: The court heard how the gang leader had tortured children for profit. The judge said she had never seen such depravity. Depravity means extreme moral corruption. Synonyms: turpitude, wickedness.

en: A person with a superficial interest in an art or field
hook: DILETTANTE: DELIGHTS in dabbling, but never goes deep.
story: Tanvir tried guitar for a week, painting for a month, and photography for two weeks. He knew a little about everything but mastered nothing. He was a dilettante. A dilettante dabbles superficially. The opposite is an expert or connoisseur.

en: Shameless boldness; insolent nerve
hook: EFFRONTERY: right in your FRONT, shamelessly.
story: The thief caught red-handed had the effrontery to demand compensation for 'wasting his time.' Everyone was speechless. Effrontery means outrageous audacity. Synonyms: temerity, gall, impudence.

en: To gradually intrude beyond proper limits
hook: EN-CROACH: like a COCKROACH creeping into your space.
story: Every year, illegal buildings encroached further onto the riverbank, until the river itself became a narrow ditch. To encroach is to gradually intrude on someone else's territory or rights. Synonyms: trespass, infringe.

en: To give a quality or ability; to provide a permanent income
hook: ENDOW: give a DOWRY of talent or money.
story: Nature endowed Sara with a beautiful voice. A wealthy alumnus endowed the university with a fund that pays for fifty scholarships every year. To endow is to give a quality or donate money for permanent support.

en: To ask someone earnestly or anxiously
hook: EN-TREAT: begging for a TREAT.
story: The mother entreated the doctor to save her son: 'Please, I'll do anything.' To entreat is to plead earnestly. Synonyms: implore, beseech, supplicate.

en: Fond of company; sociable
hook: GREGARIOUS: GREG is in every group (grex = herd).
story: Mitu is gregarious: she talks to strangers on buses, organizes every party, and knows everyone in the building. Gregarious means sociable. Sheep and elephants are gregarious animals, living in herds.

en: A formal charge of a serious crime; a strong criticism
hook: INDICTMENT (in-DITE-ment): the court DICTATES charges.
story: The prosecutor issued an indictment against the bank manager for fraud. The flood deaths were an indictment of the city's poor planning. An indictment is a formal accusation, or evidence that something is seriously wrong.

en: Angry at something unjust
hook: INDIGNANT: your DIGNITY was insulted.
story: When the shopkeeper accused Arif of stealing, he was indignant: 'I've been your customer for ten years!' Indignant means angry at unfair treatment. Indignation is righteous anger.

en: Unable to be avoided; inevitable
hook: IN-E-LUCTABLE: you can't struggle (luctari) out of it.
story: Death and taxes are ineluctable, as the old saying goes. For the old fishing village, the river's advance was ineluctable; no wall could stop it. Ineluctable means inescapable. Synonyms: inevitable, unavoidable.

en: Curious; eager for knowledge
hook: INQUISITIVE: always INQUIRING.
story: The inquisitive child asked a hundred questions a day: Why is the sky blue? Where do clouds go? Why do cats purr? Inquisitive means curious and eager to learn. It can also mean nosy about other people's business.

en: Freedom from restrictions; scope for action
hook: LATITUDE: lots of room, wide like LATITUDE lines across the globe.
story: The new manager gave her team wide latitude: work from anywhere, choose your own methods, just deliver results. Latitude means freedom of action. In geography, latitude measures distance from the equator.

en: Treating serious matters with humor or lack of respect
hook: LEVITY: LIGHT as LEVITATING.
story: During the tense meeting, the manager's joke about his own bad cooking added a moment of levity, and everyone relaxed. But levity at a funeral would be inappropriate. Levity means lightheartedness. Its opposite is gravity.

en: Wishing to do evil to others
hook: MALE-VOLENT: wishing (vol) BAD (mal).
story: In the folk tale, a malevolent witch cursed the village wells, smiling as the people suffered. Malevolent means wishing harm on others. Its opposite is benevolent.

en: To intervene to help resolve a dispute
hook: MEDIATE: stand in the MIDDLE.
story: When the two families argued over the boundary wall, the village elder mediated, listening to both sides and finding a fair compromise. To mediate is to help two sides reach agreement. A mediator is neutral.

en: To block or obstruct
hook: OCCLUDE: CLOSE it off (claudere = to close).
story: A blood clot occluded the artery, stopping blood flow to the heart. Thick clouds occluded the moon. To occlude is to block or shut off. Synonyms: obstruct, block.

en: To calm someone's anger or agitation
hook: PACIFY: make PEACE (pax), like a baby's PACIFIER.
story: The baby wouldn't stop crying until Grandma pacified her with a lullaby and a pacifier. The police tried to pacify the angry crowd. To pacify is to calm. Synonyms: placate, appease, mollify.

en: A model of excellence; a perfect example
hook: PARAGON: PARAmount, the top example.
story: Mrs. Hossain was a paragon of patience: she taught slow learners for thirty years and never once raised her voice. A paragon is a perfect example of a quality. Synonyms: exemplar, model, epitome.

en: To treat with apparent kindness that reveals a feeling of superiority; also, to be a customer of
bn: অনুগ্রহ দেখানোর ভান করা; নিয়মিত খরিদ্দার হওয়া
hook: PATRONIZE: acting like a 'PATRON' to someone below you.
story: 'Oh, you finished the whole problem by yourself? Good job, sweetie,' the senior engineer said to his fully qualified colleague. She hated being patronized. To patronize is to treat condescendingly. It can also mean to be a regular customer.

en: Extremely poor; also, extremely stingy
hook: PENURIOUS: without a PENNY.
story: The penurious student lived on one meal a day, walked everywhere to save bus fare, and studied under streetlights. Penurious means extremely poor. It can also mean stingy. Penury is extreme poverty.

en: Having a pleasantly sharp, spicy taste; stimulating and interesting
hook: PIQUANT (PEE-kunt): it PIQUES your tastebuds.
story: The street-food chotpoti was piquant: tangy tamarind, sharp chili, and a touch of black salt. The story was piquant too, full of intriguing twists. Piquant means pleasantly spicy, or stimulatingly interesting.

en: Spreading unchecked; widespread and uncontrolled
hook: RAMPANT: RAMPAGING everywhere.
story: During the monsoon, dengue was rampant: hospitals overflowed and nearly every family had a sick member. Rampant means spreading without control. Rampant corruption, rampant inflation, rampant weeds.

en: Far away; distant; slight or faint
hook: REMOTE: far away like a REMOTE village, or a remote chance.
story: The doctor traveled to a remote island village where no hospital existed. The chance of finding survivors after three days was remote. Remote means distant, or slight. A remote possibility is very unlikely.

en: An unprincipled person
hook: REPROBATE: REPROVED and BEATEN by society.
story: Uncle Jalal was the family reprobate: gambling, drinking, and borrowing money he never returned. Relatives hid their wallets when he visited. A reprobate is a morally unprincipled person. Synonyms: scoundrel, miscreant.

en: Cloudy or muddy (of liquid); confused
hook: TURBID: TURBulent water, all stirred up.
story: After the storm, the river turned turbid: brown, muddy, and full of debris. Arif's thoughts were just as turbid after the sleepless night. Turbid means cloudy with sediment, or confused. Don't confuse it with turgid.

en: Swollen; pompous and overly complex in style
hook: TURGID: TURNED rigid from swelling, swollen with big words.
story: The report's turgid prose, full of long words and endless sentences, made a simple point almost impossible to find. A sprained ankle becomes turgid with swelling. Turgid means swollen, or pompously overwritten.

en: Showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty
hook: VACUOUS: like a VACUUM, empty inside.
story: The celebrity gave a vacuous interview: 'Life is, like, about vibes, you know?' Viewers couldn't find a single thought in it. Vacuous means empty-headed. Synonyms: vapid, inane.
